item.title: MSS Celebrates 20 Years of Industry Leadership, Unveils New Brand Identity and Future Growth Vision
item.description: Nigeria’s leading event technology company, Mobile Screens and Sound Limited ( MSS ), has marked two decades of pioneering innovation, industry transformation and excellence with a landmark gala held on Thursday, October 8, at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos. The event, themed The Art of Experience, brought together an influential gathering of business leaders, government officials, industry stakeholders, clients, partners and friends of the brand to celebrate a company whose innovations have helped shape the modern events landscape in Nigeria. For 20 years, MSS has remained at the forefront of event technology, delivering the sound, visuals, staging and technical expertise behind some of Nigeria’s most significant corporate, entertainment, government and cultural events. From introducing cutting-edge LED screen technology at a time when it was largely unfamiliar to the market, to becoming one of the country’s most trusted providers of integrated event production solutions, MSS has consistently redefined what is possible in the live experiences industry. The evening showcased the company’s remarkable journey from a bold entrepreneurial venture into an industry leader whose footprint extends across every facet of event technology. Through immersive storytelling, visual displays and experiential installations, guests were taken through the evolution of MSS and the pivotal role it has played in raising industry standards and inspiring the growth of an entire ecosystem of event technology providers. Reflecting on the company’s journey, Founder and Managing Director, Tunbosun Kola-Daisi , said: “Twenty years ago, we entered an industry where the solutions we offered were largely unfamiliar and where belief in the future of event technology was limited. LED screens, which are commonplace today, were then considered a novelty. The early years tested our resilience, and it took nearly five years before we broke even. But we remained steadfast in our vision because we understood the transformative power of technology in creating unforgettable experiences. Today, as we celebrate this milestone, we are proud not only of what we have built, but of the role MSS has played in shaping an industry, creating opportunities and setting new standards for excellence.” A defining moment of the evening was the unveiling of the company’s new logo and refreshed brand identity, signalling a bold new chapter in MSS’ evolution. The rebrand reflects the company’s growth and reinforces its position as a comprehensive provider of event technology solutions spanning sound, lighting, screens, production services, and immersive audience experiences. The unveiling culminated in a spectacular drone display that illuminated the Lagos skyline, symbolising the innovation, ambition and creativity that have defined the MSS journey for two decades. But we remained steadfast in our vision because we understood the transformative power of technology in creating unforgettable experiences. Today, as we celebrate this milestone, we are proud not only of what we have built, but of the role MSS has played in shaping an industry, creating opportunities and setting new standards for excellence.” A defining moment of the evening was the unveiling of the company’s new logo and refreshed brand identity, signalling a bold new chapter in MSS’ evolution. The rebrand reflects the company’s growth and reinforces its position as a comprehensive provider of event technology solutions spanning sound, lighting, screens, production services, and immersive audience experiences. The unveiling culminated in a spectacular drone display that illuminated the Lagos skyline, symbolising the innovation, ambition and creativity that have defined the MSS journey for two decades. Speaking on the company’s future direction, Kola-Daisi added: “What began as a vision to transform event experiences has evolved into a business capable of powering some of the largest and most complex productions in Nigeria. Today, we can deliver large-scale sound reinforcement across major venues, deploy screens simultaneously across multiple events, support uninterrupted operations through an extensive power infrastructure, execute nationwide advertising installations, transform physical spaces into immersive experience centres, and provide end-to-end production management for events of every scale. But this is only the beginning. Our next chapter is focused on deeper innovation, strategic expansion across Africa and investing in the people who will drive the future of this industry. We are committed to remaining the benchmark for event technology excellence while building the next generation of industry professionals.” The anniversary celebration also highlighted MSS’ commitment to developing talent through the recently launched MSS Event Tech Academy, a pioneering capacity-building initiative designed to address the growing demand for skilled professionals within the event technology ecosystem. Delivered in partnership with KolaDaisi University, the intensive 10- week programme provided participants with both technical and practical training across six specialist areas: LED Screen Engineering, Sound Engineering, Camera Craft and Video Production, Lighting Design and Control, Event Management and Production, and Rigging and Trussing. More than 60 students completed the inaugural programme, gaining valuable hands-on experience through participation in live MSS projects and productions. Demonstrating the academy’s tangible impact, five graduates secured immediate employment with MSS upon completion of the programme. As Nigeria’s event technology industry continues to evolve, MSS remains committed to advancing professional standards, nurturing talent and driving innovation that elevates live experiences across the continent. Twenty years after helping pioneer a new era of event technology in Nigeria, MSS continues to set the pace, proving that exceptional experiences are not merely produced, but carefully engineered. About Mobile Screens and Sound Limited (MSS) Mobile Screens and Sound Limited (MSS) is Nigeria’s leading event technology company, delivering world-class solutions across sound, lighting, LED displays, staging, live production and experiential event management. With two decades of industry leadership, MSS has powered some of the country’s most notable live, corporate and entertainment events while championing innovation, professional excellence and talent development within the event technology sector. item.title: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
item.description: null The comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) discovered by the Euclid mission. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026) The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short. What is it? (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24. "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement . Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us. An close up view of comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) Why is it incredible? Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

item.title: The Glenlivet Introduces a Three-Day Immersive Experience in Lagos
item.description: Lagos has no shortage of events, but from 19 to 21 November, The Glenlivet is planning something a little different. For three nights, Lagos will host The Glenlivet Experience, a curated immersion into the heritage, craftsmanship and distinctive character of the iconic Speyside single malt Scotch whisky, brought to life through a distinctly Lagos lens. Across the three days, The Glenlivet’s Brand Ambassadors, Ebuka Obi-Uchendu , Osas Ighodaro and Farooq Oreagba, will join the brand’s Tastemakers and guests from across culture, business, fashion, music and hospitality. Evane Chenuet, Marketing Director, Pernod Ricard Nigeria, said: “We wanted people to experience The Glenlivet single malt whisky rather than simply hear about it. The Glenlivet Experience brings our rich brand’s heritage to life in a way that feels contemporary, culturally relevant and that immerses our guests in our spirit of originality .” The first two days will welcome a curated audience, while on 21st November, the Experience will extend its invitation to a wider community, offering more guests the opportunity to discover the world of The Glenlivet. The Glenlivet Experience 19–21 November 2026 5:00 PM – 11:00 PM For updates on registration and access, follow @TheGlenlivetNG on Instagram. #TheGlenlivetNG #TheGlenlivetExperience #LiveOriginal #MadeToFollowNoOne Drink Responsibly. 18+ Sponsored Content The post The Glenlivet Introduces a Three-Day Immersive Experience in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Asake, Tems, Wizkid & Ayra Starr Lead African Acts Nominated for 2027 Grammys
item.description: Tems, Asake, and Ayra Starr lead the stellar lineup of African nominees contending for Best African Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards. The Recording Academy has just rolled out the official nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards, and the Best African Music Performance category is an absolute powerhouse lineup with Nigerian artists making up a significant part of this year’s shortlist. Leading the category is Asake , who pulled off an incredible double entry in the category. He picked up a solo nod for his standout track “ Gratitude ” alongside a stellar collaborative nomination for “ Jogodo ” alongside Wizkid . For Wizkid, this latest nomination adds another major chapter to his historic Grammy legacy, building on his previous career milestones, which include his historic win for Best Music Video with Beyoncé for “ Brown Skin Girl ” at the 63rd Grammy Awards in 2021, as well as multiple past nominations. Tems is another Nigerian nominee, returning to the category she won at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025 with “ Love Me JeJe ”. This time, she is nominated for “ Big Daddy ”. Her previous Grammy win came in 2023, when she received Best Melodic Rap Performance for her contribution to Future ‘s “ Wait for U ”, featuring Drake . The Nigerian representation also includes Ayra Starr , whose nomination comes through “ Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?) ”, a collaboration with Beninese music legend Angélique Kidjo . Ayra Starr previously received a nomination in the category for “ Rush ”, while Angélique Kidjo brings her own Grammy-winning history to the collaboration, with wins for albums including Eve , Sings , Celia and Mother Nature . Rounding out the category with rich cultural resonance are Ghanaian musicians King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni , who earned a brilliant nomination for “ No Tradition, No Africa “. The 69th Grammy Awards will hold on 7 February 2027 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The post Asake, Tems, Wizkid & Ayra Starr Lead African Acts Nominated for 2027 Grammys appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.description: Nigerian actress, trained lawyer, and TFAA co-host Genoveva Umeh dressed for the 20th edition of The Future Awards Africa. Photo Credit: The Future Awards Africa/Instagram A historic hosting line-up spanning five African countries and the introduction of a first-of-its-kind AI assistant named Infinity marked the 20th edition of The Future Awards Africa (TFAA), held on Saturday, 14 November 2026, at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Themed “Celebrating The Redefiners: Africa’s AI Generation,” the ceremony recognised young Africans aged 18 to 35 across 26 categories, including technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, governance, music, film, literature, advocacy, sports and fashion. The anniversary edition was hosted by five personalities from across the continent: Nigerian actress and trained lawyer Genoveva Umeh ; Kenyan media personality Claudia Naisabwa ; Malawian radio broadcaster and television personality Priscilla Kayira ; Botswana television and radio host Resego Motlhokathari ; and Tanzanian actor and former Big Brother Africa winner Idris Sultan . Co-hosts Genoveva Umeh, Resego Motlhokathari, Claudia Naisabwa, Idris Sultan, and Priscilla Kayira pose together ahead of the 20th anniversary ceremony. Photo Credit: The Future Awards Africa/Instagram They shared the stage with Infinity, an AI assistant that interacted with the hosts through quick-witted and playful responses, drawing laughter from guests throughout the ceremony. Its introduction brought artificial intelligence into the evening’s entertainment, while musical performances by Sharp Band and the Loud Urban Choir added to the celebrations. Among the evening’s major winners, Nora Awolowo received the Prize for Young Person of the Year, Teniola Aladese won the Prize for Acting, and Olamidun Ogundoyin took home the Prize for Entrepreneurship. Pastor Jerry Uchechukwu Eze , represented at the ceremony by media personality Hero Daniels , received the Prize for Service to Young People. The ceremony also welcomed representatives of distinguished public figures, including Mobolaji Abubakre Ogunlende , Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, who represented Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu . Another highlight was the recognition of the first winners of The Future Awards Africa Independent (TFAAi), a state-level initiative established in 2026 to spotlight young changemakers whose contributions may receive limited attention on national platforms. Its first edition covered Rivers, Abia, Oyo and Kano States, extending the awards’ reach into more communities. item.title: Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch
item.description: There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result. Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so. Continue reading...

item.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
item.description: null The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated . (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.) For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated. The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service. The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future. Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur , the successor to the venerable Atlas V. Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit. The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef .

item.title: ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore’ is now streaming on Disney+, with 4 minutes of bonus footage and a special ‘Doomsday’ preview
item.description: null Disney and Marvel Studios have a lot riding on " Avengers: Doomsday, " and they’re pulling out all the stops to make sure audiences are well-prepared to experience the alt-universe battle royale when it drops on December 18. After a successful limited theater run earlier this fall, Marvel Studios just dropped "Avengers: Endgame Encore" onto Disney+. So, if you missed this beefed-up extended rerelease in theaters, you can still experience all the extra content that ties directly into the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday." "Endgame's" recent theatrical return came on Sept. 25, 2026, earned $86 million, and included four bonus scenes totaling roughly four minutes and a special "Doomsday" preview. The rerelease also took it back to the pinnacle of the all-time box office peak by passing "Avatar." The $356 million sequel to 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War" closed out The Infinity Saga, and the two-part spectacle became widely known as the high-water mark of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. "Avengers: Endgame Encore" will also be included in Disney+'s signature "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" collection, a curated roundup of former Marvel shows and movies to study up on. If you haven't been keeping up with the MCU, you've got plenty of homework to do ahead of "Avengers: Doomsday." "Avengers Endgame: Encore' is now streaming on Disney+. (Image credit: Marvel Studios) With its charismatic cast of dozens and the triumphant MCU return of Robert Downey Jr., this time portraying the metal-masked Victor Von Doom, expectations are sky-high that this might reignite the glory days and usher in a brave new world for bored superhero-loving cinephiles. "Avengers: Endgame Encore" is now on Disney+. Watch Avengers: Endgame Encore on Disney+: Disney+ (With Ads): $11.99/month Disney+ Premium (No Ads): $18.99/month or $189.99/year

item.title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
item.description: null We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets. But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic. "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule." As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't." Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions. 130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA) In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth . Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth. What is the Astra Carta? The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility. Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart. "I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022. item.content:encoded: null We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets. But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic. "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule." As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't." Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions. 130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA) In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth . Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth. What is the Astra Carta? The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility. Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart. "I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022. The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield. What does the Astra Carta say? "It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness." To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space. "If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?" King Charles III (middle) is photographed in discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield (right) at Buckingham Palace. (Image credit: Photo by EAMONN M. MCCORMACK/POOL/AFP via Getty Images) The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords . Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures. But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more. From paper to action Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them. "What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose." To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield. The Astra Carta seal on display at a UKSA event. (Image credit: Photo by Chris Jackson/Getty Images) The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX . It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center , Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman , Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors. In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework. "The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page". The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades. The Astra Carta seeks to place sustainability at the core of space exploration, protecting Earth in the process. (Image credit: Joshua Stevens/NASA Earth Observatory) "The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enf

item.title: A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46
item.description: Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence. But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was , not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion. item.title: Tiyani Makamu Wins Miss South Africa 2026!
item.description: Tiyani Makamu celebrates on stage moments after being crowned Miss South Africa 2026 at the Sandton Convention Centre in Johannesburg on 14 November 2026. Photo Credit: Miss South Africa/Instagram South Africa has a new queen, and her name is Tiyani Makamu ! At a stylish finale held at the Sandton Convention Centre in Johannesburg on Saturday, 14 November 2026, the 27-year-old entrepreneur and youth advocate from Bronkhorstspruit, Gauteng stepped forward to claim the Miss South Africa 2026 crown. Outgoing titleholder Qhawekazi Mazaleni handed over the reins, while Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo from Edenvale and Lesego Khumo Nyathela from Springs took home the First Princess and Second Princess titles. Away from the pageant stage, Tiyani Makamu already wears plenty of impressive hats. A graduate of the Pearson Institute of Higher Education, she works as a communications professional, Group Digital Lead, and Client Success Executive, and also runs Hubsela—a small-business support platform she founded to help fellow entrepreneurs build thriving ventures. Her passion for youth employment and business education also shows up in her community work, including supporting a local library initiative in Ivory Park to help young people gain practical skills. Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu, entrepreneur and founder of Hubsela from Bronkhorstspruit, Gauteng. Photo Credit: Miss South Africa/Instagram What makes Tiyani Makamu’s reign especially exciting is how different Miss South Africa 2026 looks this year. Under the Motsepe Group of Companies’ ownership, the Miss South Africa Organisation shifted its focus toward homegrown leadership and social impact—meaning neither Makamu nor her runners-up will head off to international competitions like Miss Universe, Miss World, or Miss Supranational. Instead, she gets to pour her entire year into community projects across South Africa through the pageant’s Empower Youth Africa initiative, backed by a R1 million cash prize and access to up to R500,000 from the Impact Fund. Chatting shortly after her crowning at the Sandton Convention Centre—which hosted the finale for the first time after four years in Pretoria—Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu shared what she hopes to accomplish over the next twelve months: My mandate as Miss South Africa is to empower women entrepreneurs by bridging the gaps in access to opportunities, business development and funding. I want to equip women with the skills, resources and financial readiness to build sustainable, thriving businesses. Through entrepreneurship and skills development, I aim to champion the economic empowerme nt of women and youth across Afr ica. Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu, who will dedicate her reign to domestic entrepreneurship and youth empowerment across South Africa. Photo Credit: Tiyani Makamu/Instagram The post Tiyani Makamu Wins Miss South Africa 2026! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?
item.description: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City Continue reading...

item.title: Celebrating African Music, Culture and Connection! Here’s a Rundown of My SIMA 2026 Experience
item.description: In the words of a sage, the reason we go and come back is so that we have tales to tell. Last week, I told you I was headed to Cotonou and invited you to come along. If you followed on Instagram, well done! Now, I must tell you even more tales of this journey! Welcome, my dear BNers, to my entire rundown of the amazing SIMA 2026, which was held in Cotonou, Benin Republic. From November 12–13, 2026, Cotonou, Republic of Benin, hosted the third edition of the Salon des Industries Musicales d’Afrique Francophone (SIMA), bringing together artists, music executives, creatives, policymakers and industry professionals from across Africa and beyond. This year’s theme, African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence , explored an important question: How do we translate the global influence of African music into sustainable economic opportunities for the people and industries behind it? As someone who loves music and storytelling, I was particularly excited to experience these conversations firsthand and share them with you. So let’s get into it. First things first, Bonjour Cotonou! View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Now, let’s get into Day 1 of SIMA. I decided to channel my inner choir girl with my black-and-white ensemble and my DIY necktie, giving a nod to the essence of the event — music. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) If you still don’t get the full picture, I break down what SIMA really is all about here. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) I went on to experience very enlightening conversations amongst industry professionals and experts. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) One of my conversations was with Mamby Diomandé , Founder and Co-Founder of SIMA, who shared insights into the vision behind the platform and its continued expansion. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) I also caught up with the Executive Director of Livespot, Solomon Sonaiya. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Now, this was one part of SIMA 2026 that particularly caught my attention. A panel presented a baseline study of women in the Nigerian music industry. And even more exciting was the official launch of VERA, a network dedicated to women in the music industry, alongside its VERA Mentorship Programme. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Now, let’s get into Day 2! From the music to even more insightful conversations, it’s safe to say I had a ball! item.title: Here Are Six Simple Ways to Prepare for the New Year
item.description: In less than 50 days, 2026 will be over. In January, a new year and Christmas that seemed like a long time away are now around the corner. Once Christmas is over, everyone begins to prepare for the new year and write down things they hope to achieve in 2027. As there will be people moving on to new adventures, getting married, moving homes and countries, starting a new job, there will be people who arrive in the new year with no fully shaped plan. Essentially, it is not because they are clueless or fail to prepare for new adventures; sometimes you just don’t have plans. You just don’t know what to expect in the coming year. As it is popularly known, “He who fails to prepare, prepares to fail.” That only works in schools where, when you don’t prepare for examinations, you might fail. In life, the logic might not exactly apply. You can prepare and still fail; you might not prepare at all and still win. Yet, it is still important to prepare, just for the sake of it; just because you can and you should. Now, preparation in this context is not a grand master plan. It is not some motivational kit that will prepare you for success in 2027. The preparation here is the simple things that you can do to be ready for a new year. Sometimes, 9-5 workers have no idea what they’ll do at work, but they sure know they have to get ready and prepare for work. Even na just one email dem go send throughout the day, they have to prepare for work. That could be applied here too. What are the simple ways you can prepare for the new year? Clean your house Whether you live alone or still at your parents’, you never know how cleaning and rearranging your house can prepare you for the coming year. Even if you sweep your house daily, rearranging your furniture, moving things around, and changing the general look of your house can build emotional preparation. It also gives your house a different look, unfamiliar to what you’re familiar with. Human beings evolve, and while the phrase “new year, new me” always sounds cliché, it can be true. We are not who we were many years ago. Also, whether you work from home or in an office, give your working environment a little attention. Reconnect with people Adulthood is a full-time job folded into other full-time jobs. We get so caught up in its web and cycle that we forget to check on people important to us. December is the best time to reconnect with people adulthood might have kept you from properly connecting with. Call your friends. Call your family members. Arrange a visit or have a proper conversation with an old friend. Call people for the sake of calling. Review your finances and your year Money is important. The amount of money one has in the bank account at the end of the year can define how big one dreams or expects the coming year to be. Even if you sweep your house daily, rearranging your furniture, moving things around, and changing the general look of your house can build emotional preparation. It also gives your house a different look, unfamiliar to what you’re familiar with. Human beings evolve, and while the phrase “new year, new me” always sounds cliché, it can be true. We are not who we were many years ago. Also, whether you work from home or in an office, give your working environment a little attention. Reconnect with people Adulthood is a full-time job folded into other full-time jobs. We get so caught up in its web and cycle that we forget to check on people important to us. December is the best time to reconnect with people adulthood might have kept you from properly connecting with. Call your friends. Call your family members. Arrange a visit or have a proper conversation with an old friend. Call people for the sake of calling. Review your finances and your year Money is important. The amount of money one has in the bank account at the end of the year can define how big one dreams or expects the coming year to be. As the year winds down, it is the best time to reflect on how the year has been personally, professionally and financially. Check your subscriptions. Cancel services you no longer use. Make a list of things you enjoyed this year. Not just achievements, but experiences, people, books, places and little moments that made you happy. Reflect on the moments from the year, good and bad, your wins, your losses, big or small, your earnings and expenditure and the consequences of your decisions. These reflections will prepare you for the new year. Settle outstanding responsibilities Think about the little things you’ve been postponing. Perhaps you need to renew an important document, address a health issue, fix a leaking tap, update your CV, return something you borrowed or finally resolve an issue you’ve been avoiding. This is for me as much as it is for you. You don’t have to enter January with every problem solved, but attending to some of these things can make the transition into a new year easier. Clear out your wardrobe You probably have clothes you haven’t worn in two years, shoes you no longer like and bags that have been hung for many years. This is a good time to sort through them. Give away clothes that are still in good condition but no longer fit you, repair the ones that need fixing and identify those you genuinely need. Decluttering the wardrobe is like letting no longer needs to be in your life, what you need to shed off as you emerge into a new year. Most importantly, rest Take a break. Sleep. Spend time with people you love. Watch your favourite films. Allow yourself to do absolutely nothing for a while. You don’t want to enter January already exhausted from trying to make December count. item.title: NASA's interstellar Voyager 1 probe is about to reach 1 light-day from Earth after nearly 50 years in space
item.description: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan , executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane. An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Howell
item.content:encoded: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan , executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane. An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return. NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said. Flying into the black Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission. "It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp." Voyager 1 officially entered interstellar space on Aug. 25, 2012. (Image credit: Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library/Getty Images) While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here." The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going. Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

item.title: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
item.description: Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world. The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino . Continue reading...

item.title: Wunmi Adelusi: Why Are We Still Hiding That We Use AI?
item.description: Not long ago, I finished a piece of writing I was proud of — my thoughts, my argument, my structure. I had used an AI tool to help tighten the grammar and smooth the flow. And then, before sharing it, I went hunting through the text to delete every long dash. Why? Because the em dash has become the internet’s favourite “tell” that AI was involved. I was, quite literally, editing my work to hide a tool I had every right to use. When I caught myself doing it, I had to laugh. And then I had to ask: why the shame? It turns out I am not alone. Across a study spanning 47 countries, 57% of employees admit to concealing how they use AI at work. The reasons are almost entirely about reputation. In one recent survey of 5,000 desk workers, nearly half said they worried about appearing less capable or less competent, and a third feared they would simply look lazy. We are using the tools, and quietly scrubbing the fingerprints. There is even a quiet hypocrisy to it. Another survey says out of 7,200 adults, 46% said they would not disclose AI’s role in their own work while the remaining 54% said other people should. I had assumed this reticence was a particularly African trait. In my own experience, my colleagues in DC and Europe — my manager included — are refreshingly matter-of-fact about it. In one meeting recently, when asked to find a specific document in a shared folder, my manager cheerfully said he’d just let AI search it rather than disturb anyone’s work. Someone joked about his “secret agent,” and we all laughed. It was open, unbothered, upfront. I had concluded that we, of African descent, were simply more conservative, more inclined to glorify the heavy lifting, to wear “I stayed up all night doing it myself” as a badge of honour. But the research corrected me. This isn’t cultural; it’s universal. Employees across the US, UK, Europe, Latin America, Japan and Australia hide their AI use at strikingly similar rates. Even leadership does it. In some studies, managers conceal their AI use more than junior staff do. So perhaps the real question is why do we treat AI-assisted work as less credible than work done the hard way? I’ve even heard of recruiters downgrading CVs that look AI-generated, penalising the polish itself. But surely the more useful question is whether the substance behind it is real. A candidate who used a tool to sharpen how they present genuine experience hasn’t cheated; they’ve shown resourcefulness. The due diligence should be on verifying the claims, not on detecting the dashes. Screening out the tell, rather than testing the truth, risks rejecting capable people for the crime of being efficient. Because when you think about it, the logic is backwards. Using AI well is not a shortcut that replaces thinking; it is a skill that reveals it. You cannot get something excellent out of these tools without putting something substantial in. A vague mind produces vague prompts and vague results. Some of the people I am most impressed by at
item.dc:creator: Wunmi Adelusi
item.content:encoded: Not long ago, I finished a piece of writing I was proud of — my thoughts, my argument, my structure. I had used an AI tool to help tighten the grammar and smooth the flow. And then, before sharing it, I went hunting through the text to delete every long dash. Why? Because the em dash has become the internet’s favourite “tell” that AI was involved. I was, quite literally, editing my work to hide a tool I had every right to use. When I caught myself doing it, I had to laugh. And then I had to ask: why the shame? It turns out I am not alone. Across a study spanning 47 countries, 57% of employees admit to concealing how they use AI at work. The reasons are almost entirely about reputation. In one recent survey of 5,000 desk workers, nearly half said they worried about appearing less capable or less competent, and a third feared they would simply look lazy. We are using the tools, and quietly scrubbing the fingerprints. There is even a quiet hypocrisy to it. Another survey says out of 7,200 adults, 46% said they would not disclose AI’s role in their own work while the remaining 54% said other people should. I had assumed this reticence was a particularly African trait. In my own experience, my colleagues in DC and Europe — my manager included — are refreshingly matter-of-fact about it. In one meeting recently, when asked to find a specific document in a shared folder, my manager cheerfully said he’d just let AI search it rather than disturb anyone’s work. Someone joked about his “secret agent,” and we all laughed. It was open, unbothered, upfront. I had concluded that we, of African descent, were simply more conservative, more inclined to glorify the heavy lifting, to wear “I stayed up all night doing it myself” as a badge of honour. But the research corrected me. This isn’t cultural; it’s universal. Employees across the US, UK, Europe, Latin America, Japan and Australia hide their AI use at strikingly similar rates. Even leadership does it. In some studies, managers conceal their AI use more than junior staff do. So perhaps the real question is why do we treat AI-assisted work as less credible than work done the hard way? I’ve even heard of recruiters downgrading CVs that look AI-generated, penalising the polish itself. But surely the more useful question is whether the substance behind it is real. A candidate who used a tool to sharpen how they present genuine experience hasn’t cheated; they’ve shown resourcefulness. The due diligence should be on verifying the claims, not on detecting the dashes. Screening out the tell, rather than testing the truth, risks rejecting capable people for the crime of being efficient. Because when you think about it, the logic is backwards. Using AI well is not a shortcut that replaces thinking; it is a skill that reveals it. You cannot get something excellent out of these tools without putting something substantial in. A vague mind produces vague prompts and vague results. Some of the people I am most impressed by at work are often the ones who prompt AI brilliantly, who feed it sharp, well-framed inputs and get back something genuinely useful. That is not a sign they did less work, but that they thought clearly about what they wanted. So how do we move from hiding to owning? A few things I am learning to practise: Disclose simply, without apology. A lecturer in my doctoral programme put it well: “Even when you use AI only to refine, add a brief note that the ideas and perspectives are mine; AI assisted with structure, editing or grammar.” It isn’t an apology. It’s integrity. It marks clearly where your thinking ends, and the tool begins. Own the thinking, not just the output. The credibility of your work rests on the judgement behind it. Be able to explain your argument, defend your choices, and stand behind every claim, whether or not a tool helped you polish it. AI should sharpen your voice, not replace it. Use it to do more, not to do less. The goal isn’t to offload the work; it’s to free yourself for higher-value thinking. When AI handles the search, the first draft, the formatting, you have more room for the judgment only you can bring. Keep your discretion. Not every tool is safe for every input. Be thoughtful about what you feed into AI, confidential or proprietary information deserves real care. Owning your AI use also means using it responsibly. Finally, stop scrubbing the fingerprints. When I use AI to strengthen my work, I will say so, without feeling it makes me look less intelligent, less hardworking, or less capable. Because knowing how to use a powerful tool well, and being honest about it, is exactly the kind of judgement the future of work will reward. So tell me, what has your experience been? Do you own up to it, or quietly scrub the fingerprints too? *** Featured Image by PNW Production for Pexels. item.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
item.description: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros. item.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
item.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

item.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
item.description: Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it. As Guardian Australia reported in September , Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare. Continue reading...

item.title: 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
item.description: null You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026. The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully. In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!). Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars. So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) "Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena. Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996. While " Independence Day " saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure. (Image credit: Warner Bros Pictures) Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result. Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. While " Independence Day " saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure. (Image credit: Warner Bros Pictures) Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result. Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs… Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status. Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly . "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.” It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got. (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory. MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks! Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them. (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's " Disclosure Day " from a few months ago. In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet. This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka! "Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
item.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: The Macallan Unveils A Night on Earth: The First Light in Nigeria
item.description: The Macallan , the renowned single malt Scotch whisky, officially launched “A Night on Earth: The First Light in Nigeria” at an exclusive event held at the Radisson Blu, Victoria Island, Lagos. The launch introduced the fourth release in the brand’s limited-edition A Night on Earth series, with retail partners Booze.ng, Drinks.ng, Barrels and Naijaliquor and others supporting its presence in the Nigerian market ahead of the festive season. The launch brought the story behind The First Light to life, introducing guests to an expression inspired by the first sunrise of the New Year in New Zealand, one of the first places in the world to welcome the occasion. The release explores the anticipation of new beginnings and the significance of shared moments, themes that resonate with the festive season as people prepare to reconnect with loved ones, celebrate milestones and look ahead to the year to come. Guiding guests through the experience was Yinka Adepetu , The Macallan Brand Educator and Ambassador, who walked them through the inspiration, design and whisky-making craft behind the release. His presentation offered insight into the details that shape The First Light, from its connection to New Zealand’s New Year traditions to the choices behind its distinctive presentation and flavour profile. The fourth expression in the series carries its story through a three-layer gift box designed by New Zealand-born artist Bonnie Brown. The artwork captures the transition from dusk to dawn, with crimson bonfires, deep blue fireworks and the amber glow of first light. Together, these elements reflect the atmosphere of New Year celebrations and the anticipation that comes with a fresh start, making the presentation an integral part of the release’s identity. The whisky itself reflects The Macallan’s approach to cask selection and maturation. Matured in sherry-seasoned American and European oak casks, alongside casks that previously held bourbon, the expression presents notes of sweet oak, vanilla, caramelised marshmallows and a hint of Manuka honey on the nose. The palate develops with berry compote, rich caramel, vanilla ice cream and stone fruits, followed by a finish of gentle spice and mellow oak. Speaking on the launch, Hammed Adebiyi , Senior Brand Manager, West and Central Africa,Edrington Portfolio, said: “A Night on Earth: The First Light brings together the craftsmanshipthat defines The Macallan and a story that speaks to the significance of new beginnings. Inspired by the first sunrise of the New Year in New Zealand, this release celebrates the moments we share and the traditions we create with the people who matter to us. We are pleased to introduce this latest chapter of the series to Nigeria as the festive season approaches, a time when togetherness, reflection and thoughtful gifting take on particularmeaning.” With its Nigerian debut, A Night on Earth: The First Light extends The Macallan’s exploration of the relationship between whisky-making, ar
